chunks: What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from Abū Ayyūb al-Khazzāz, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: The tashahhud in salat (prayer)? He said: Twice. He said: I said: And how is it twice? He said: When you have settled sitting, then say: I bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, having no partner, and I bear witness that Muḥammad is His servant and His Messenger; then you depart. He said: I said to him: The servant’s saying, “All greetings are for Allah, and the salats and the good things are for Allah”? He said: This wording is from du'a (supplication) by which the servant speaks gently to his Lord.

key_terms.أَشْهَدُ: I bear witness; the core verbal formula of testimony
key_terms.التَّحِيَّاتُ: greetings or salutations, mentioned here as part of a supplicatory expression
key_terms.التَّشَهُّدُ: the testimony recited while seated in salat (prayer)
key_terms.الدُّعَاءِ: supplication, describing the status of the additional wording
key_terms.الصَّلَاةِ: the ritual salat (prayer) in which tashahhud is recited
key_terms.رَسُولُهُ: His Messenger, affirming the messengership of Muḥammad صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
key_terms.مَرَّتَيْنِ: twice, indicating the number of tashahhuds in the prayer context asked about

ai.seo_question: What is the minimum tashahhud that suffices in salat (prayer)?
ai.summary: This hadith explains the obligation of tashahhud in salat (prayer) and identifies its minimum sufficient form. It also clarifies that additional phrases such as “al-taḥiyyātu lillāh...” belong to du'a (supplication), serving as a gentle address by the servant to his Lord.
